blocks: The graph is the upper half of the ellipsoid \(4x^2+y^2+z^2=16\), with \(z\ge0\).

questions.text: Let \(f(x,y)=\ln(y-x^2)\), with the additional restriction \(y\le4\). Find the domain, its projection onto the \(x\)-axis, and the range. Find the maximum and all points where it occurs. Does a smallest value exist? Justify your answer.

For \(0\le k<\sqrt a\), the level curve is the circle \(x^2+y^2=a-k^2\). For \(k=\sqrt a\), it is \((0,0)\). All other levels are empty.

process_requests(stock, ["bolt", "bolt", "nut", "pin"], [3, 3, 2, 1])
=> ([True, False, True, False], {"bolt": 2, "nut": 0})

questions.title: From a configuration to chemical behavior
body: Data: An atom X has configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s²4p³. Atomic numbers: As 33, Se 34, Br 35, Kr 36.
(a) Identify X, its period, group, and number of valence electrons. (b) Give its unpaired-electron count. (c) Write X³⁻ and Se²⁻ configurations. (d) Are those ions isoelectronic, and which is larger?

blocks: (a) As; period 4; group 15; 5 valence electrons. (b) 3. (c) Both [Kr], or [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s²4p⁶. (d) Yes; As³⁻ is larger.

questions.title: Inert-pair and pseudo-noble-gas configurations
body: Data: Sn has Z = 50 and neutral configuration [Kr] 4d¹⁰5s²5p². Use the lecture terminology: inert pair = retained ns²; pseudo-noble-gas configuration = filled d subshell beneath empty outer s and p subshells.
(a) Write Sn²⁺ and Sn⁴⁺ configurations. (b) Assign the two terms to the appropriate ions. (c) Are either ions isoelectronic with a noble gas? (d) Classify both magnetically.

blocks: (a) Sn²⁺: [Kr] 4d¹⁰5s²; Sn⁴⁺: [Kr] 4d¹⁰. (b) Sn²⁺: inert pair; Sn⁴⁺: pseudo-noble-gas. (c) Neither. (d) Both diamagnetic.

questions.title: Radius comparisons with different electron counts
body: Data: Z(S) = 16, Cl = 17, K = 19, Ca = 20, Fe = 26. Use the usual main-group radius trends and isolated-ion comparisons.
(a) Rank S²⁻, Cl⁻, K⁺, Ca²⁺ from largest to smallest. (b) Rank K, Ca, and Br atoms from largest to smallest. (c) Which is larger in each pair: Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ and Cl/Cl⁻?

blocks: (a) S²⁻ > Cl⁻ > K⁺ > Ca²⁺. (b) K > Ca > Br. (c) Fe²⁺; Cl⁻.

questions.title: Successive ionization and exceptions
body: Data: A period-3 element has successive ionization energies 578, 1817, 2745, and 11,577 kJ/mol. Candidate elements: Na, Mg, Al, Si. For the last part, use: IE₁(Be) = 900, IE₁(B) = 801, IE₁(N) = 1402, IE₁(O) = 1314 kJ/mol.

(a) Identify the period-3 element and its usual ion charge. (b) Find the energy to form 0.125 mol gaseous 3+ ions from its gaseous atoms. (c) Which member of each Be/B and N/O pair has the higher IE₁? Identify the relevant subshell or electron-pairing effect.

blocks: (a) Al; +3. (b) 643 kJ. (c) Be > B: removal of B’s higher-energy 2p electron. N > O: electron pairing in O’s 2p subshell.

questions.title: Electron affinity signs and electron transfer
body: Data: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻ requires 496 kJ/mol. Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g) has ΔE = −349 kJ/mol. Ignore attraction between the separated product ions.

(a) Find ΔE for Na(g) + Cl(g) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g). (b) Is the separated-ion process endothermic or exothermic? (c) Would the process O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g) ordinarily require or release energy? (d) Does the result in (a) prove that forming NaCl(s) from the gaseous atoms is endothermic?

questions.title: What a radius measurement means
body: Data: The Cl–Cl covalent bond length is 198 pm. The closest Cl···Cl distance between separate nonbonded molecules is 360 pm. In a simple additive covalent-radius model, the C–Cl distance is 176 pm.
(a) Estimate the covalent and van der Waals radii of Cl. (b) Estimate the carbon covalent radius. (c) Which chlorine radius should be used to estimate a C–Cl bond length?

questions.title: Connect the models to the evidence
body: Select every true statement about atomic structure and electromagnetic radiation.
choices: Diffraction supports the wave behavior of light and electrons.
A quantum-mechanical orbital is a definite circular path around the nucleus.
For fixed n in a multielectron atom, greater penetration usually lowers orbital energy.
A continuous range of arbitrary bound electron energies explains an atomic line spectrum.
Across a main-group period, increasing effective nuclear attraction generally reduces atomic radius.
Higher light amplitude can increase intensity without changing frequency or photon energy.
In Planck’s oscillator model, energy exchanges occur in integer multiples of hν rather than arbitrary amounts.

questions.title: Bonding models and electrical conduction
body: Data: Consider pure solid Cu, solid NaCl, molten NaCl, aqueous NaCl, and pure liquid CH₃OH. Dissolved NaCl is fully dissociated; methanol is a molecular nonelectrolyte.

(a) Classify the primary bonding model of Cu, NaCl, and CH₃OH. (b) Which listed samples conduct well, and what particles carry charge? (c) Why can an ionic crystal be brittle even though its attractions are strong?

blocks: (a) Metallic; ionic; covalent within molecules. (b) Solid Cu: mobile electrons; molten/aqueous NaCl: mobile ions. Solid NaCl and pure methanol do not conduct well. (c) Layer displacement can place like-charged ions adjacent, causing repulsion.

questions.title: Lattice energy: charge versus separation
body: Data: Use the simplified comparison U ∝ |z₊z₋|/r, where r is ion-center separation. NaCl: charges ±1, r = 282 pm; MgO: charges ±2, r = 212 pm; KBr: charges ±1, r = 329 pm. Ignore differences in crystal geometry. U means positive energy required to separate the solid into gaseous ions.
(a) Rank lattice-energy magnitudes. (b) Estimate U(MgO)/U(NaCl). (c) Give the sign of the reverse lattice-formation energy.

questions.title: Bond length is not bond strength
body: Data: Compare bonds between the same pair of atoms where possible. For sulfur–halogen bonds, use the atomic-size trend F < Cl < Br.
(a) Rank C–C, C=C, and C≡C in increasing length and increasing strength. (b) Rank S–F, S–Cl, S–Br in increasing length. (c) Is a double bond necessarily exactly twice as strong as a single bond?

blocks: (a) Length: C≡C < C=C < C–C. Strength: C–C < C=C < C≡C. (b) S–F < S–Cl < S–Br. (c) No.

questions.title: Bond dipoles and ionic character
body: Data: Electronegativity values H 2.1, C 2.5, N 3.0, O 3.5, F 4.0. Use ΔEN to compare polarity; do not impose a sharp universal ionic/covalent cutoff.
(a) Rank C–H, N–H, O–H, and H–F in increasing bond polarity. (b) Label δ⁺ and δ⁻ on each bond. (c) Rank the same bonds in decreasing percent ionic character.

blocks: (a) C–H < N–H < O–H < H–F. (b) H is δ⁺ in all four; C, N, O, or F is δ⁻. (c) H–F > O–H > N–H > C–H.

questions.title: Lewis structure versus oxidation numbers
body: Data: Valence electrons: C 4, O 6. For oxidation numbers, assign both electrons of each C–O bond to O. Use the lowest-formal-charge octet structure for CO.
(a) Draw CO with every lone pair and formal charge. (b) Give the oxidation number of each atom. (c) Give bond order, σ/π counts, and the total valence-electron count.

blocks: (a) ⁻:C≡O:⁺; one lone pair on each atom; FC(C) = −1, FC(O) = +1. (b) C +2; O −2. (c) Bond order 3; 1 σ and 2 π; 10 valence electrons.

questions.title: Equivalent resonance and fractional bond order
body: Data: Valence electrons N 5, C 4, O 6; add electrons for negative charge. Require octets for N, C, and O.

For NO₃⁻ and CO₃²⁻: (a) draw all equivalent major resonance forms, (b) give every atom’s formal charge in one form, (c) give the average central–O bond order, and (d) give the number of distinct central–O bond lengths in the actual ion.

blocks: NO₃⁻: 24 electrons; three equivalent forms, each with one N=O and two N–O⁻ bonds. FC: N +1; double-bonded O 0; each single-bonded O −1. Average N–O bond order 4/3; one N–O length.
CO₃²⁻: 24 electrons; three equivalent forms, each with one C=O and two C–O⁻ bonds. FC: C 0; double-bonded O 0; each single-bonded O −1. Average C–O bond order 4/3; one C–O length.
In each form: double-bonded O has 2 lone pairs; each single-bonded O has 3; central atom has none.

questions.title: Unequal resonance contributors
body: Data: NCO⁻ has fixed connectivity N–C–O and 16 valence electrons. Consider octet forms A: N≡C–O, B: N=C=O, and C: N–C≡O. Complete lone pairs. Electronegativity O > N > C.
(a) Give (FC on N, C, O) for each form. (b) Rank their importance using formal-charge rules. (c) Is it justified to take an unweighted mean of all three bond orders as the exact actual bond order?

questions.title: A nitrogen oxide with asymmetric bonding
body: Data: N₂O has connectivity N–N–O and 16 valence electrons. Consider octet structures A: N≡N–O and B: N=N=O. O is more electronegative than N.
(a) Supply all lone pairs and formal charges in A and B. (b) Which is the more important contributor? (c) Predict the central atom’s molecular geometry and hybridization using the lecture model.

blocks: A: terminal N has 1 lone pair, central N 0, O 3; formal charges (terminal N, central N, O) = (0, +1, −1). B: terminal N has 2 lone pairs, central N 0, O 2; charges = (−1, +1, 0). (b) A. (c) Linear; sp.

questions.title: Three different octet exceptions
body: Data: Valence electrons B 3, N 5, O 6, F 7, P 5, Cl 7. Consider BF₃, NO₂, and PCl₅ as individual molecules.

(a) Count total valence electrons and classify the octet exception for each. (b) Which must contain an unpaired electron? (c) Could replacing P by N produce an ordinary five-single-bond Lewis structure for NCl₅ with an allowed expanded octet?

blocks: (a) BF₃: 24, electron-deficient B; NO₂: 17, odd-electron radical; PCl₅: 40, expanded valence shell on P. (b) NO₂. (c) No.

questions.title: Oxyacid structures and formal charges
body: Data: H₃PO₄ has P bonded to four O atoms; three O atoms each bear one H. Total valence electrons = 32. Compare an all-single-bond P–O structure with a structure having P=O to the O without H.

(a) Assign formal charges to every type of atom in both structures. (b) Which structure is preferred by the formal-charge rules used in lecture? (c) Give the electron-group arrangement and ideal O–P–O angle in both.

blocks: (a) All single bonds: P +1; O without H −1; all O–H oxygens and all H atoms 0. With P=O: every atom 0. (b) The P=O structure. (c) Tetrahedral; 109.5° ideal in both.

questions.title: One workflow, four molecular shapes
body: Data: Valence electrons Be 2, B 3, N 5, O 6, Cl 7, F 7, H 1. Use isolated BeCl₂ molecules rather than the solid polymer.
For BeCl₂, BF₃, NH₃, and H₂O, give (a) central-atom bonding/lone-pair counts, (b) electron-group arrangement, (c) molecular shape, (d) approximate bond angle, and (e) lecture-model hybridization.

blocks: BeCl₂: 2 bonds/0 lone pairs; linear; linear; 180°; sp. BF₃: 3/0; trigonal planar; trigonal planar; 120°; sp². NH₃: 3/1; tetrahedral; trigonal pyramidal; about 107° (<109.5°); sp³. H₂O: 2/2; tetrahedral; bent; about 104.5° (<109.5°); sp³.

questions.title: Five electron groups do not mean five bonds
body: Data: Valence electrons S 6, Cl 7, Xe 8, F 7. Use the expanded-valence and hybridization labels from lecture.

For SF₄, ClF₃, and XeF₂: (a) give total valence electrons, AXₘEₙ notation, electron-group arrangement, and molecular shape; (b) place the central lone pairs in axial or equatorial positions; (c) give the lecture-model hybridization; (d) identify which molecule has zero net dipole.

blocks: SF₄: 34 e⁻, AX₄E, trigonal bipyramidal, seesaw, one equatorial lone pair, sp³d. ClF₃: 28 e⁻, AX₃E₂, trigonal bipyramidal, T-shaped, two equatorial lone pairs, sp³d. XeF₂: 22 e⁻, AX₂E₃, trigonal bipyramidal, linear, three equatorial lone pairs, sp³d. (d) XeF₂ only.

questions.title: Six electron groups and cancellation
body: Data: Valence electrons Br 7, Xe 8, S 6, F 7. Use the lecture-model hybridization labels.

For BrF₅, XeF₄, and SF₆, give central lone-pair count, molecular shape, ideal bond-angle families, hybridization, and polar/nonpolar classification. For XeF₄, state the relative positions of the lone pairs.

blocks: BrF₅: 1 lone pair; square pyramidal; approximately 90° and 180° families (distorted from ideal); sp³d²; polar. XeF₄: 2 opposite lone pairs; square planar; 90° and 180°; sp³d²; nonpolar. SF₆: 0 lone pairs; octahedral; 90° and 180°; sp³d²; nonpolar.

questions.title: Multiple bonds and nonideal angles
body: Data: COCl₂ has structure O=CCl₂ with two C–Cl single bonds and no lone pair on C. A double-bond electron group repels adjacent bonding groups more strongly than a single-bond group.

(a) Give the number of electron groups on C and its geometry. (b) Predict whether Cl–C–Cl is smaller or larger than 120°, and whether O–C–Cl is smaller or larger than 120°. (c) Count σ and π bonds. (d) Would counting the double bond as two VSEPR groups be correct?

blocks: (a) 3; trigonal planar. (b) Cl–C–Cl <120°; O–C–Cl >120°. (c) 3 σ, 1 π. (d) No.

questions.title: Same geometry, different molecular polarity
body: Data: CO₂ is O=C=O; COS is O=C=S; both are linear. CCl₄ and CHCl₃ are tetrahedral. Use EN(C) = EN(S) = 2.5, EN(O) = 3.5, EN(Cl) = 3.0, EN(H) = 2.1.

(a) Classify each molecule as polar or nonpolar. (b) Give the direction of the net bond-dipole arrow in COS. (c) Is “all linear molecules are nonpolar” true? (d) Is a polar bond sufficient by itself to guarantee a polar molecule?

blocks: (a) CO₂ nonpolar; COS polar; CCl₄ nonpolar; CHCl₃ polar. (b) Toward O. (c) No. (d) No.

questions.title: Hybridization and overlap in acetone
body: Data: Acetone is CH₃–C(=O)–CH₃. Use the localized hybridization model in the slides.
(a) Give the hybridization of each C and of O. (b) Count all σ and π bonds, including C–H. (c) Identify the orbitals that form the C=O σ bond and π bond. (d) Give the geometry around each carbon.

blocks: (a) Each CH₃ carbon sp³; carbonyl C sp²; O sp². (b) 9 σ, 1 π. (c) σ: C(sp²)–O(sp²); π: side-by-side overlap of unhybridized p orbitals. (d) CH₃ carbons tetrahedral; carbonyl C trigonal planar.

questions.title: Triple bonds, double bonds, and rotation
body: Data: Acrylonitrile has connectivity H₂C=CH–C≡N. Each H has one bond, and N has one lone pair.

(a) Give the hybridization of the three carbon atoms in order and of N. (b) Count all σ and π bonds. (c) How many unhybridized p orbitals on the nitrile carbon participate in π bonding? (d) Can the C=C bond rotate freely while retaining its π overlap?

blocks: (a) sp², sp², sp; N sp. (b) 6 σ, 3 π. (c) 2. (d) No.

questions.title: Bond-energy estimate and a limiting reagent
body: Data: C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g). Average bond energies (kJ/mol): C=C 614, C–C 347, H–H 436, C–H 413. Molar masses: C₂H₄ 28.05 g/mol; H₂ 2.016 g/mol. Use ΔH ≈ ΣBE(broken) − ΣBE(formed). Assume complete reaction and ignore heating of the products.
(a) Estimate ΔH per mole of C₂H₄ reacted. (b) When 5.610 g C₂H₄ reacts with 0.3024 g H₂, identify the limiting reagent and estimate the heat released. (c) Does breaking a bond itself release energy?

blocks: (a) −123 kJ/mol. (b) H₂; 18.5 kJ released (q for the reaction = −18.5 kJ). (c) No.

questions.title: Hydrogen bonding: donor versus acceptor
body: Data: Methanol CH₃OH, dimethyl ether CH₃OCH₃, methylamine CH₃NH₂, and CH₃F each have the usual Lewis structure. Use the introductory course rule: H bonding involves H bonded to N, O, or F; O/N lone pairs can accept H bonds. Do not treat carbon-bound F as a conventional aqueous H-bond acceptor in this question.

(a) Which can hydrogen-bond to identical molecules in a pure sample? (b) Which of methanol, ether, and methylamine can accept a hydrogen bond from water? (c) Identify every IMF present in pure liquid ether. (d) Which end of water points toward Na⁺ in solution?

blocks: (a) Methanol and methylamine. (b) All three. (c) London dispersion and dipole–dipole. (d) The oxygen end.

questions.title: Boiling point and vapor pressure rankings
body: Data: Ethanol CH₃CH₂OH and dimethyl ether CH₃OCH₃ both have molar mass 46.07 g/mol. Propane CH₃CH₂CH₃ has molar mass 44.10 g/mol. Consider comparable liquid samples at the same temperature where all have measurable equilibrium vapor pressures.

(a) Rank normal boiling points from lowest to highest. (b) Rank equilibrium vapor pressures from lowest to highest. (c) Name the strongest characteristic IMF in each molecular liquid; all three also have dispersion.

blocks: (a) Propane < dimethyl ether < ethanol. (b) Ethanol < dimethyl ether < propane. (c) Propane: dispersion; ether: dipole–dipole; ethanol: hydrogen bonding.

questions.title: Polarizability and molecular contact
body: Data: n-Pentane and neopentane are nonpolar C₅H₁₂ isomers; n-pentane is elongated, neopentane compact. Cl₂ and Br₂ are nonpolar; Br₂ has the larger, more polarizable electron cloud.

(a) Predict the higher boiling point in each pair. (b) Do the pentane isomers have equal boiling points merely because their molar masses match? (c) Does the existence of a permanent dipole always make a small molecule boil higher than any nonpolar molecule?

questions.title: Cis/trans polarity and phase changes
body: Data: In cis-1,2-dichloroethene, the two Cl atoms lie on the same side of C=C; in the trans isomer they lie on opposite sides. Both are planar, have the same formula and molar mass, and have equivalent C–Cl bond dipoles.

(a) Classify each as polar/nonpolar and identify which has the higher boiling point. (b) Is its higher boiling point evidence of a stronger C=C bond? (c) When either liquid boils without decomposition, are C–Cl bonds broken?

blocks: (a) Cis polar, trans nonpolar; cis has the higher boiling point. (b) No. (c) No.

questions.title: Phase-change energy and mass
body: Data: At 0°C, ΔHfus(H₂O) = 6.01 kJ/mol; at 100°C, ΔHvap(H₂O) = 40.65 kJ/mol. M(H₂O) = 18.015 g/mol. Ignore heat loss. Each part is a separate constant-temperature phase-change experiment.

(a) How much heat is absorbed when 27.02 g ice melts at 0°C? (b) What mass of steam at 100°C must condense to release the same magnitude of heat? (c) Give signs of ΔH for sublimation, deposition, and freezing. (d) During melting of pure ice at fixed pressure, does added heat raise the temperature while both phases remain?

questions.title: Dynamic equilibrium in a sealed flask
body: Data: A sealed flask contains a pure liquid and its equilibrium vapor at fixed temperature. In parts (a)–(c), enough liquid remains to maintain liquid–vapor equilibrium; assume an ideal vapor.

(a) Are evaporation and condensation stopped or occurring at equal rates? (b) The headspace volume doubles at constant temperature. After equilibrium returns, what happens to vapor pressure and vapor moles? (c) Would adding more of the same liquid change equilibrium vapor pressure? (d) If all liquid evaporates and only gas remains, must its pressure still equal the saturation vapor pressure?

blocks: (a) Occurring at equal rates. (b) Vapor pressure unchanged; vapor moles double. (c) No. (d) No.

questions.title: Predict a new vapor pressure
body: Data: A liquid has vapor pressure 115.0 torr at 35.00°C and ΔHvap = 38.56 kJ/mol, assumed constant. R = 8.31446 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹; T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.
(a) Calculate its vapor pressure at 55.00°C using the two-point Clausius–Clapeyron equation. (b) At 55.00°C, would it boil under an external pressure of 250.0 torr?

questions.title: Find the boiling temperature under reduced pressure
body: Data: A liquid has Pᵥₐₚ = 150.0 torr at 30.00°C and constant ΔHvap = 34.00 kJ/mol. External pressure is 450.0 torr. R = 8.31446 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹; T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.
(a) Find its boiling temperature in °C. (b) Would its normal boiling point be higher or lower?

questions.title: Infer enthalpy and the normal boiling point
body: Data: A pure liquid has vapor pressure 80.00 torr at 25.00°C and 240.0 torr at 50.00°C. Assume constant ΔHvap. R = 8.31446 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹; normal boiling pressure = 760.0 torr.
(a) Determine ΔHvap in kJ/mol. (b) Predict the normal boiling point in °C. (c) Give the slope of a plot of ln(P) versus 1/T, with T in K.

questions.title: What changes at altitude?
body: Data: Compare the same pure liquid at sea level and on a mountain. The mountain has lower atmospheric pressure. For parts (c)–(d), compare samples at the same liquid temperature.

(a) Where is the boiling point lower? (b) Is the normal boiling point itself redefined by moving the sample uphill? (c) Is equilibrium vapor pressure lower solely because external atmospheric pressure is lower? (d) Would a sample with stronger IMFs generally have higher or lower vapor pressure at that temperature?

blocks: (a) On the mountain. (b) No. (c) No. (d) Lower.

questions.title: Read a carbon dioxide phase diagram
body: Data: CO₂ triple point ≈ −56.6°C, 5.11 atm; critical point ≈ 31.0°C, 73.0 atm; sublimation point at 1.00 atm ≈ −78.5°C. The schematic is not to scale.

(a) Name the phase change when solid CO₂ is heated at 1.00 atm through −78.5°C. (b) Can liquid CO₂ be an equilibrium phase at 1.00 atm? (c) What three phases coexist at the triple point? (d) Classify CO₂ at 40.0°C and 90.0 atm. (e) At 40.0°C, can pressure alone create a distinct ordinary liquid phase?

blocks: (a) Sublimation. (b) No. (c) Solid, liquid, and gas. (d) Supercritical fluid. (e) No.

questions.figureAlt: Schematic pressure–temperature phase diagram. All numerical coordinates needed are supplied in the question; curves are not to scale.

questions.title: Why water’s melting line slopes backward
body: Data: Near 0°C, ice is less dense than liquid water. Water’s solid–liquid coexistence line has negative slope on a pressure–temperature phase diagram. Consider small pressure changes near ordinary ice–water conditions.

(a) At fixed temperature near the melting boundary, does increasing pressure favor ice or liquid? (b) Does increasing pressure raise or lower the melting point? (c) Would the same melting-point trend be expected for a substance whose solid is denser than its liquid? (d) Name the gas → solid phase change.

blocks: (a) Liquid. (b) Lower. (c) No; a positive melting-line slope is usual in that case. (d) Deposition.

questions.title: Phases, motion, and the critical point
body: Select every true statement. Assume ordinary molecular solids and liquids.
choices: Particles in a solid have zero kinetic energy.
A liquid has a nearly fixed volume but takes the shape of the part of the container it occupies.
A liquid and its vapor in one container can be two phases of one pure substance.
Above the critical temperature, enough pressure always produces a distinct liquid–gas boundary.
Strong intermolecular attractions favor condensed phases; thermal motion favors dispersal.

questions.title: Vapor-pressure correction meets gas stoichiometry
body: Data: At 25.00°C, Pᵥₐₚ(H₂O) = 23.76 torr. Assume ΔHvap(H₂O) = 44.00 kJ/mol is constant over this interval. R = 8.31446 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ for Clausius–Clapeyron and 0.082057 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ for gases. 1 atm = 760 torr. M(Mg) = 24.305 g/mol.

A 0.5000 L sample of H₂ collected over water at 40.00°C has total pressure 745.0 torr and equal water levels inside and outside the collector. The H₂ is produced by Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g), with excess acid.
(a) Estimate the water vapor pressure at 40.00°C. (b) Find dry H₂ pressure. (c) Find the mass of Mg that reacted. Assume ideal gases and negligible H₂ solubility.

questions.title: A rectangle and an exponential
body: Evaluate \(\iint_R xe^y\,dA\), where \(R=[0,2]\times[0,\ln3]\). Give an iterated integral in each order.

questions.title: Average value versus total
body: Let \(f(x,y)=x^2+2y\) on \(R=[-1,1]\times[0,3]\). Find (a) its integral over R and (b) its average value. (c) Find the integral of \(x^3+xy\) over the same region.

questions.title: Midpoints and accuracy
body: Approximate \(\iint_{[0,2]\times[0,2]}(x^2+y^2)\,dA\) using four equal square subrectangles and their midpoints. Then find the exact value and the signed error “approximation minus exact.”

blocks: Midpoint approximation: \(10\). Exact value: \(32/3\). Signed error: \(-2/3\), an underestimate.

questions.title: An order that makes integration possible
body: Reverse the order of \(\int_0^1\int_x^1 e^{y^2}\,dy\,dx\), then evaluate it.

questions.title: A sloping ceiling
body: Find the volume between \(z=x+y\) and \(z=4\) above the triangle \(x\ge0\), \(y\ge0\), \(x+y\le2\). Give a double integral and its value.

questions.title: One region, two descriptions
body: Let D have vertices \((0,0),(2,0),(1,1)\). Write \(\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA\) in each order, splitting if needed. Also find the area of D.

questions.title: Annular accumulation
body: Use polar coordinates to evaluate \(\iint_D(x^2+y^2)\,dA\), where \(1\le x^2+y^2\le4\). Also find the average value of \(x^2+y^2\) on D.

questions.title: A disk away from the origin
body: Let \(D=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le2x\}\). Give polar bounds and evaluate \(\iint_Dx\,dA\).

questions.title: Average distance in a quarter disk
body: Find the average distance from the origin of points in the first-quadrant quarter disk \(x^2+y^2\le4\), using a uniform area average.

questions.title: A nonuniform triangular lamina
body: A plate occupies \(x\ge0,y\ge0,x+y\le2\) and has density \(\delta(x,y)=x\). Find its mass and center of mass.

questions.title: Axis names matter
body: A rectangular plate \(0\le x\le2,0\le y\le1\) has constant density 3. Find its mass, \(I_x\), \(I_y\), and its radius of gyration about the x-axis.

questions.title: Probability on a curved event region
body: Textbook extension: A joint probability density is \(p(x,y)=c(x+y)\) on \([0,1]\times[0,1]\) and zero elsewhere. Find c and \(P(Y\ge X^2)\).

questions.title: Tilted area
body: Find the area of the part of \(z=2x-y+3\) above the triangle \(x\ge0,y\ge0,x+y\le2\).

questions.title: A paraboloid patch
body: Find the curved surface area of \(z=(x^2+y^2)/2\) for \(x^2+y^2\le4\). Do not include a flat cap.

questions.title: Choose a graph carefully
body: Find the curved area of the upper half of the cylinder \(x^2+z^2=4\), between \(y=0\) and \(y=3\). Exclude the end caps. Give the surface-area integral using \(z=f(x,y)\); interpret endpoint singularities as improper limits.

questions.title: A tetrahedron and a weighted total
body: Let \(E=\{x,y,z\ge0:x+y+z\le2\}\). Find (a) its volume, (b) \(\iiint_Ez\,dV\), and (c) its centroid.

questions.title: Reorder nested inequalities

guides.title: Functions of several variables
body: Domain: impose every restriction simultaneously. Square roots require a nonnegative radicand; logarithms require a positive argument; denominators cannot be zero.
Use solid boundaries for included points and dashed boundaries for excluded points. Keep the original restrictions when squaring or solving for a level.
The range is the set of attained output values. Check endpoints rather than assuming they are included.
Level curves satisfy \(f(x,y)=k\); level surfaces satisfy \(f(x,y,z)=k\). They live in input space. Vertical traces use \(x=a\) or \(y=b\).
For equal height steps, closer contours indicate steeper change. Check the labels and scale.

guides.title: Brief continuity review
body: Continuity at \((a,b)\) requires \(\lim_{(x,y)\to(a,b)}f(x,y)=f(a,b)\), through every path in the domain.
Two paths with different limits prove that the limit does not exist. Agreement along a few paths does not prove that a limit exists.
For continuous elementary functions, substitute directly where the expression is defined.
Partial derivatives can exist even when the function is not continuous; see question 14.3.8.

guides.title: Partial derivatives
body: Hold the other variables constant and apply the usual product, quotient, and chain rules.
\(f_x\) and \(f_y\) are coordinate trace slopes, not function heights.
\(f_{xy}=(f_x)_y\). Continuous mixed second partials can be interchanged. Differentiate repeatedly before substituting a point.
If \(F(x,y,z)=0\) defines \(z\) locally and \(F_z\ne0\), then \(z_x=-F_x/F_z\) and \(z_y=-F_y/F_z\).
When computing \(F_x,F_y,F_z\), hold the other inputs constant. When differentiating the identity, remember that \(z\) depends on \(x,y\).
Existence of partial derivatives alone does not guarantee continuity or differentiability.

guides.title: Tangent planes and linear approximations
body: Linearization: \(L(x,y)=f(a,b)+f_x(a,b)(x-a)+f_y(a,b)(y-b)\). The tangent plane is \(z=L(x,y)\).
Differential: \(df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy\), with an additional \(f_z\,dz\) term for three inputs.
\(\Delta f\) is the exact new value minus the old value; \(df\) approximates it.
Estimated maximum error: \(|df|\le|f_x|\varepsilon_x+|f_y|\varepsilon_y\). Relative error is \(|df|/|f|\); multiply by \(100\) for a percentage.
Continuous first partials near the point guarantee differentiability. A zero partial means no first-order contribution, not necessarily zero actual change.

guides.title: Chain rule and related rates
body: Along a path, \(df/dt=f_xx'+f_yy'+f_zz'\).
For two parameters, \(f_s=f_xx_s+f_yy_s+f_zz_s\), and similarly for \(f_t\). Include every dependency path.
In \(G(u(s,t),v(s,t))\), evaluate the outer derivatives \(G_u,G_v\) at \((u,v)\), not at \((s,t)\).
For \(F(x,y)=0\), implicit differentiation gives \(y'=-F_x/F_y\) when \(F_y\ne0\).
Use signed rates and consistent units in related-rate problems. With explicit time dependence, \(dT/dt=T_xx'+T_yy'+T_t\).
Change per unit time and change per unit distance are different quantities.

guides.title: Directional derivatives and gradients
body: The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives. For a unit vector \(\mathbf u\), \(D_{\mathbf u}f=\nabla f\cdot\mathbf u\).
Toward \(Q\) from \(P\), normalize \(Q-P\) before taking the dot product.

Maximum rate: \(\|
abla f\|\), in direction \(
abla f/\|
abla f\|\). Minimum rate: \(-\|
abla f\|\), in the opposite direction. Perpendicular directions have zero rate.
For \(F=c\) with nonzero gradient, the tangent plane is \(\nabla F(P)\cdot(\mathbf r-P)=0\); the normal line is \(\mathbf r=P+t\nabla F(P)\).
Along a path, \(df/dt=\nabla f\cdot\mathbf r'\). A zero directional derivative at one point does not make a straight path a level curve.

guides.title: Local and absolute extrema
body: Critical points satisfy \(f_x=f_y=0\), or occur where a partial is undefined. A candidate need not be an extremum.
With continuous second partials, let \(D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-(f_{xy})^2\).
If \(D>0\) and \(f_{xx}>0\): local minimum. If \(D>0\) and \(f_{xx}<0\): local maximum. If \(D<0\): saddle. If \(D=0\): inconclusive.
A continuous function on a closed bounded region attains absolute extrema. Check interior candidates, every boundary segment, and endpoints; compare original function values.
When \(D=0\), use signs, factorization, sums of squares, or paths. State the extremal values and all attaining points.
A nonstrict minimum permits nearby points with equal values; a strict minimum does not.

guides.title: Top-down design and dictionaries
body: Start with the whole goal, divide it into coherent major tasks, and refine each task until its implementation is clear. Sibling tasks should have distinct responsibilities. Several reasonable decompositions may exist.

Root: no parent. Node: any element. Parent/child: adjacent levels. Leaf: no children. A leaf does not have to be on the deepest level. Hierarchies manage complexity but can hide connections across branches.

A dictionary maps keys to values. Keys are unique; values may repeat. d[key] looks up a key, not a position. Assigning an existing key replaces its value; assigning a new key adds a pair. Accessing a missing key raises KeyError.

key in d checks exact keys, not values or substrings. for key in d iterates over keys; use d[key] to read each corresponding value. len(d) counts pairs. Update existing values freely; avoid adding/deleting keys while directly iterating over the dictionary.
Initialize a missing key once; update on every occurrence. Do not reset a count each time you see the key.

Lecture 8 teaches {}, key indexing/assignment, membership, and direct iteration. This bank does not require get, items, values, pop, dictionary comprehensions, or other methods from a broader dictionary guide.
Source: Lecture8.pdf pp11-18,19-25,28-32

guides.title: Functions, scope, and shared objects
body: def records a function; its body runs when called. Parameters are the local names in the header; arguments are supplied at the call. return immediately exits the function. print displays text; it does not substitute for returning a result. Reaching the end without return gives None.
return a, b returns one tuple. x, y = f() unpacks by position. Tuple indexing and slicing work, but replacing a tuple slot raises TypeError. A mutable list stored inside a tuple can still change.

Each call gets local parameter/variable bindings. Reassigning a numeric or string parameter does not change the caller variable. A function can read a global if not shadowed; assigning to a name makes it local unless declared global. Reading such a local before assigning it raises UnboundLocalError.

a[0] = 9 changes a shared list; a = [9] only rebinds local a. For lists, a += [9] mutates while a = a + [9] rebinds. Dictionaries also share mutations through passed references. b = a aliases a list; b = a[:] makes a new outer list, not a recursive copy of nested lists.

Omitted trailing arguments use defaults; an explicit zero does not. In the taught positional headers, required parameters precede defaulted ones. Put a docstring first in the body describing purpose, inputs, outputs, and relevant units. Prefer arguments and returned results over hidden global dependencies.

Bind arguments -> run the body in order -> track shared-object mutations separately -> stop at return -> assign/use the returned object in the caller. Keep a separate row of local variables for every call.

guides.title: Atomic structure & periodic trends
body: Use this guide before or after the 20 Chapter 6 questions. The review emphasizes multistep reasoning at roughly past-exam difficulty, with a few harder combinations and no unmarked off-syllabus units.

sections.title: Light, spectra, and photons
body: \(c=\lambda\nu\), \(E_{\rm photon}=h\nu=hc/\lambda\). Convert wavelength to meters before using SI constants. Shorter wavelength → higher frequency → higher photon energy. Spectrum from low to high energy: radio, microwave, infrared, visible (red → violet), ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

Amplitude affects intensity, not frequency. Diffraction/interference reveal wave behavior; quantized energy exchange and the photoelectric effect reveal photon behavior. A hot object’s broad spectrum differs from an isolated atom’s discrete absorption/emission lines.
Photon count: \(N=E_{\rm total}/E_{\rm photon}\). A light source of power P delivers energy \(Pt\). Energy per mole of photons is \(N_AE_{\rm photon}\).

Planck’s quantization model restricts an oscillator’s energy to integer multiples of hν: E = nhν. Energy is exchanged in discrete quanta rather than arbitrary amounts; this resolves the classical failure to describe blackbody radiation. Distinguish this oscillator n from the hydrogen principal quantum number in the Bohr formula.

sections.title: Photoelectric effect
body:

u_0=\phi/h\), \(\lambda_0=hc/\phi\). Ejection requires \(
